source_basis: Official strategy documentation lists negative shift as a future-data lookahead pattern.
Official strategy documentation warns that whole-dataframe aggregations let a signal candle see future candles.
Official strategy documentation warns against absolute iloc indexing inside populate methods because full backtest data are present.
Official strategy documentation warns that default resample labeling can move data from an hour boundary to the start of the hour.
Official strategy documentation gives a trailing rolling mean as the non-biased alternative to a whole-dataframe mean.
Official strategy documentation recommends shift to access a previous candle rather than absolute indexing.
pandas documents bfill as using the next valid observation; NoFutureData classifies that as future use when row order is time.
pandas documents ffill as propagating the last valid observation forward, which is causal for time-ordered rows.

Official cross-validation guidance says classical KFold/ShuffleSplit assumptions are inappropriate for time-series data because train/test observations can remain unreasonably correlated. This reproduction carries explicit time-series context that the source-only scanner does not infer.
context: X is a time-ordered event log and this splitter is used for model evaluation.

source_basis: The cross_val_score API documents that None or an integer cv selects KFold or StratifiedKFold; scikit-learn's time-series guidance explains why classical folds are inappropriate when observations are time ordered.
context: X and y are time ordered and cross_val_score is used to estimate future predictive performance.

source_basis: Official GroupKFold documentation states that groups appear in arbitrary order throughout the folds. For a panel whose rows remain time ordered within entities, group separation alone does not enforce chronological train-before-test evaluation.
context: Rows are a panel time series grouped by entity; GroupKFold is used for forecasting evaluation without an additional chronological split.

source_basis: Official GroupShuffleSplit documentation describes randomized train/test partitions over groups. In panel forecasting, randomized group partitions do not by themselves impose chronological train-before-test ordering.
context: Rows are a panel time series grouped by entity; GroupShuffleSplit is used for forecasting evaluation without an additional chronological split.

source_basis: The official learning_curve API is a metadata-routing-capable model-selection router and documents that None or an integer cv selects KFold or StratifiedKFold. For explicitly time-ordered data, those folds do not enforce train-before-test chronology.
context: X and y are time ordered and learning_curve is used to evaluate future predictive performance.
source: sizes, train, test = learning_curve(model, X, y, cv=5)

source_basis: The official validation_curve API supports metadata routing and documents that None or an integer cv selects KFold or StratifiedKFold. On explicitly time-ordered data, parameter validation with those folds can train on observations later than a validation fold.
context: X and y are time ordered and validation_curve is used for temporal model selection.
source: train, test = validation_curve(model, X, y, param_name='alpha', param_range=[0.1, 1.0], cv=5)

source_basis: The official permutation_test_score API supports metadata routing and documents that None or an integer cv selects KFold or StratifiedKFold. Its cross-validated score therefore inherits the same chronology problem when the dataset is explicitly time ordered.
context: X and y are time ordered and permutation_test_score is used to assess a forecasting model.
source: score, perm, p = permutation_test_score(model, X, y, cv=5)

source_basis: TimeSeriesSplit is designed for time-ordered data. Passing it explicitly to learning_curve makes the chronological evaluation contract visible in source.
source: sizes, train, test = learning_curve(model, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48))

source_basis: TimeSeriesSplit is designed for time-ordered data. Passing it explicitly to validation_curve provides a chronological control for parameter validation.
source: train, test = validation_curve(model, X, y, param_name='alpha', param_range=[0.1, 1.0], cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48))

source_basis: TimeSeriesSplit is designed for time-ordered data. Passing it explicitly to permutation_test_score prevents its cross-validation stage from silently selecting ordinary IID folds.
source: score, perm, p = permutation_test_score(model, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48))

source_basis: Official time-related feature-engineering guidance uses TimeSeriesSplit with a gap to preserve temporal evaluation order.
The TimeSeriesSplit API is designed for time-ordered data; passing it explicitly to cross_val_score makes the temporal evaluation contract visible in source.
source: scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48))

source_basis: The official nested-CV example establishes an inner GridSearchCV and outer cross_val_score structure. On explicitly time-ordered data, using integer/default IID folds at both levels can train and tune on future observations, so both calls are context-gated.
context: X and y are time ordered; GridSearchCV is the inner model-selection loop and cross_val_score is the outer generalization estimate.
source:
search = GridSearchCV(model, params, cv=5)
scores = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=5)

source_basis: TimeSeriesSplit is designed for time-ordered data. Supplying it explicitly to both the inner GridSearchCV and outer cross_val_score makes both levels of the nested temporal evaluation contract visible.
source:
search = GridSearchCV(model, params, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=24))
scores = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=24))

source_basis: Official Polars Series.shift documentation says a negative n shifts in the opposite direction and is similar to SQL LEAD; on time-ordered rows this exposes later values to earlier rows.
Official Polars documentation describes positive shift as similar to SQL LAG, so a positive one-row shift is a causal previous-row control for ordered data.

Official Xarray DataArray.shift documentation states that negative offsets shift data to the left while coordinates stay in place. On a dimension explicitly named time, shift(time=-1) exposes a later observation at an earlier timestamp.
The same Xarray API defines positive offsets as shifting to the right. On a time dimension, shift(time=1) is the paired previous-observation control.

Official NumPy roll documentation defines circular element shifts; a negative shift moves later elements toward earlier positions. In explicitly time-ordered data this is a future dependency, so the opt-in time-series context detects the narrow NumPy attribute-call form.
context: values is time ordered and the rolled array is used as a historical feature.

source_basis: A positive roll moves prior values forward; explicitly masking the wrapped first element removes the circular future value and provides a causal lag control for time-ordered rows.
Official Dask Series.shift documentation states that periods may be positive or negative; on time-ordered rows, a negative one-row shift exposes the next observation to the current row.
The same Dask API documents positive periods; a positive one-row shift is the paired previous-row control for time-ordered data.
Official PySpark pandas Series.shift documentation states that periods can be positive or negative; on time-ordered rows, a negative one-row shift exposes the next observation to the current row.
The same PySpark pandas API documents positive periods; a positive one-row shift is the paired previous-row control for ordered data.

Official PySpark pandas Series.diff documentation accepts negative periods and shows a negative-period example as a difference with the following value; on ordered rows that introduces a future dependency.
The same PySpark pandas documentation defines the default positive period as comparison with the previous row, providing the paired causal control.
Official Snowpark pandas Series.shift documentation states that periods can be positive or negative and includes a negative-period example that moves later values into earlier rows.
The same Snowpark pandas API documents positive periods; a positive one-row shift is the paired previous-row control for time-ordered data.
Official Snowpark pandas Series.diff documentation accepts negative periods and demonstrates diff(periods=-1); on ordered rows that compares with the following observation.
The same Snowpark pandas documentation defines positive periods against previous rows, providing the paired causal control.
